newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour unlikely to opt for EMU launch entry - FT.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour unlikely to opt for EMU launch entry - FT.

text.p: Britain's main opposition Labour Party is preparing European Union states for a British decision not to join the first wave of European monetary union in 1999, the Financial Times daily reported on Wednesday.
But the party says this does not undermine its claims to be more positive towards Europe than the government.

Robin Cook, Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, said he had already discussed the problem with leading figures in European centre-left parties, which are in government in 11 of the other 14 EU nations.
Britain takes over the EU presidency in the first half of 1998, when EU governments will determine which have met the convergence criteria for joining EMU.
Labour are favourites to win an election which British Prime Minister John Major must call by May.
"Several indicated to me they could see some attractions in having a neutral chairman on single currency issues," Cook told the Financial Times. "They don't think it will be a problem."
He added: "Labour will take a constructive approach to the EU. Under the Conservatives we are getting the worst of all worlds. We are in a union while constantly sounding as if we wished we weren't."

Cook, who has rarely disguised his scepticism towards EMU, said the cabinet's decision to pit the Conservatives against early EMU membership had made it harder for a future Labour government to meet a 1999 timetable.
"I have never understated those difficulties. If anything they have been made more difficult by last week's statement by the government," he said.
Cook said Britain under Labour would use the EU presidency to push for EU enlargement and completion of the single market.
He described as one of his main objectives overseeing "the very difficult and delicate task of identifying" which east and southern European states will be eligible to join.
Britain would also push the EU Commission to crack down on remaining protectionist practices in the telecommunications, defence and financial services sectors. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7767
